title: 2 Kings 24:1–7
context: Jehoiakim becomes Nebuchadnezzar’s servant for three years and then rebels, and the LORD sends raiding bands against Judah according to the word spoken by his prophets. The narrator explains the invasions as the LORD’s judgment for the sins of Manasseh and the innocent blood he shed (cf. 21:10–16; 23:26–27), and Jehoiakim’s reign closes with Egypt no longer able to oppose Babylon. Both traditions read this frame as shared ground about judgment already announced, and 2 Chronicles 36:6 reports that Nebuchadnezzar bound Jehoiakim to take him to Babylon, a detail Kings does not record; interpreters discuss how that notice relates to this account.

verses.text: In his days Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came up, and Jehoiakim became his servant for three years. Then he turned and rebelled against him.
verses.arminianNotes:
“In his days Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came up, and Jehoiakim became his servant for three years. Then he turned and rebelled against him.” Arminian readers note that Jehoiakim’s rebellion is a political choice with real consequences.

The narrator does not give his reasons, and the exact dates are debated.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also see Jehoiakim acting as a responsible king, whose choices unfold within the judgment the LORD had already announced.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the political events of Judah’s last years are presented as part of the LORD’s word coming to pass (24:2).

verses.text: The LORD sent against him bands of the Chaldeans, bands of the Syrians, bands of the Moabites, and bands of the children of Ammon, and sent them against Judah to destroy it, according to the LORD’s word which he spoke by his servants the prophets.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The LORD sent against him bands of the Chaldeans, bands of the Syrians, bands of the Moabites, and bands of the children of Ammon.” Arminian readers note that the narrator names the LORD as the one acting through these nations.

The judgment comes “according to the LORD’s word which he spoke by his servants the prophets” (cf. 21:10–15).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see God’s sovereign hand directing the nations as instruments of judgment.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the LORD warned through his prophets before acting, and the nations remain responsible for their own violence.

verses.text: Surely at the commandment of the LORD this came on Judah, to remove them out of his sight for the sins of Manasseh, according to all that he did,
verses.arminianNotes:
“Surely at the commandment of the LORD this came on Judah, to remove them out of his sight for the sins of Manasseh.” Arminian readers note that the narrator traces the exile to a long history of persistent sin (cf. 23:26–27).

Judgment came after generations of warning, not suddenly.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the LORD’s commandment as the decisive cause behind the historical events.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: Judah’s later kings continued in the evil that Manasseh began (24:9, 19), so the judgment falls on a people who shared in that sin.

verses.text: and also for the innocent blood that he shed; for he filled Jerusalem with innocent blood, and the LORD would not pardon.
verses.arminianNotes:
Manasseh “filled Jerusalem with innocent blood, and the LORD would not pardon.” Arminian readers note the weight Scripture gives to the shedding of innocent blood (cf. 21:16).

2 Chronicles 33:12–13 records Manasseh’s personal repentance, yet the national consequences were not withdrawn.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God’s justice in refusing to overlook bloodshed that had filled the city.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground and a sober warning: God’s patience is real, but persistent, unrepented injustice brings judgment on a community.

verses.text: Now the rest of the acts of Jehoiakim, and all that he did, aren’t they written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah?
verses.arminianNotes:
“Now the rest of the acts of Jehoiakim, and all that he did, aren’t they written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah?” Arminian readers note the standard closing formula for a king’s reign.

The narrator refers readers to another record for further detail.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also note the formula, which places Jehoiakim’s reign within the continuing record of Judah’s kings.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the book selects what serves its account of the LORD’s dealings with his people.

verses.text: So Jehoiakim slept with his fathers, and Jehoiachin his son reigned in his place.
verses.arminianNotes:
“So Jehoiakim slept with his fathers, and Jehoiachin his son reigned in his place.” Arminian readers note the brief notice of his death.

2 Chronicles 36:6 says Nebuchadnezzar bound him to carry him to Babylon, and Jeremiah 22:18–19 announces a dishonorable burial; how these relate is an open question.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise note that the accounts of Jehoiakim’s end differ in detail, and they leave the question unresolved.

Both traditions treat the succession as shared ground: the throne passes to his son, though only for a short time.

verses.text: The king of Egypt didn’t come out of his land any more; for the king of Babylon had taken, from the brook of Egypt to the river Euphrates, all that belonged to the king of Egypt.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The king of Egypt didn’t come out of his land any more; for the king of Babylon had taken, from the brook of Egypt to the river Euphrates, all that belonged to the king of Egypt.” Arminian readers note that Judah can no longer look to Egypt for help.

The shift in power is often connected with Jeremiah 46:2.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the LORD’s purpose advancing through the rise of Babylon.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: alliances Judah had relied on cannot shield it from the judgment the LORD had announced.
